questions.scenario: Scenario: Code Generation with Claude Code. Your team uses Claude Code for code generation, refactoring, debugging and documentation, and is wiring it into the development workflow with custom slash commands, skills and CLAUDE.md configuration.
questions.stem: A tech lead wrote a `/release-notes` command that drafts release notes from merged PRs, and saved it as `~/.claude/commands/release-notes.md` on their own laptop. Two new engineers cloned the repository this week, and in their sessions `/release-notes` is not recognized. The lead wants every current and future team member to get the command, with changes reviewed through the normal pull request process. What is the BEST fix?

options.text: Add a section to the project CLAUDE.md that describes the release-notes steps, so Claude follows them whenever someone asks for release notes.
Send the file to each engineer and ask them to copy it into their own `~/.claude/commands/` directory during onboarding.
Move the file to `.claude/commands/release-notes.md` inside the repository and commit it, so it is shared through version control.
Register the command in a `.claude/config.json` file with a `commands` array that points at the lead's original markdown file.

questions.explanation: Commands (and skills) under the project's `.claude/commands/` or `.claude/skills/` directory are checked into the repo, so everyone who clones it gets `/release-notes`, and changes go through code review. `~/.claude/commands/` is the **user** scope: it only exists on that one machine. Current docs fold commands into skills (`.claude/skills/release-notes/SKILL.md` also creates `/release-notes`); either project location meets the requirement.

whyWrong.A: CLAUDE.md is always-loaded context, not a command definition. It does not create a `/release-notes` slash command, and it adds that procedure to every session's context even when nobody needs it.
whyWrong.B: Manual copying works for today's engineers, but it is not version controlled: future hires miss it, copies drift apart, and edits skip PR review.
whyWrong.D: Claude Code has no `.claude/config.json` with a `commands` array. Commands are discovered from directories, not registered in a config file.

questions.mindset: Team-wide = project scope in the repo; personal = home directory.

questions.scenario: Scenario: Developer Productivity with Claude. You are building developer productivity tooling on Claude Code and the Agent SDK that helps engineers explore unfamiliar codebases, understand legacy systems, generate boilerplate and automate repetitive tasks using the built-in tools and MCP servers.
questions.stem: Your team built a `/map-module` skill that walks a legacy module, reads dozens of files and prints a long inventory of classes, call paths and TODOs before giving a short architectural summary. Engineers like the summary, but after one run the main session is full of file listings, and later answers in the same session get noticeably worse. The team wants the most reliable fix that keeps the skill's behaviour and needs the fewest changes to how engineers work. What should you do?

options.text: Add `context: fork` to the skill's SKILL.md frontmatter so it runs in an isolated subagent and only its final result returns to the main conversation.
Add an instruction to SKILL.md telling Claude to keep its output short and to avoid printing intermediate file listings while it works.
Ask engineers to run `/compact` after every `/map-module` run so the verbose inventory is summarized before they continue working.
Move the skill's instructions into the project CLAUDE.md so Claude already knows the analysis procedure and does not need to load the skill.

questions.explanation: `context: fork` runs the skill in a separate subagent context: Claude Code starts a subagent, hands it the skill content as its prompt, and the verbose file reads happen there. Only the subagent's result comes back to the main conversation (by default it runs in the background and the result arrives when it finishes). The docs and exam guide name this as the way to keep verbose output such as codebase analysis out of the main session, and it is a single frontmatter change. One caveat: the forked subagent does not see the conversation history, so the skill's instructions must stand on their own, which a self-contained module walk already does.

whyWrong.B: A brevity instruction is advisory and fights the job itself: the skill has to read many files, and those tool results land in context however short the final answer is.
whyWrong.C: `/compact` is a manual cleanup that every engineer must remember, it summarizes away other useful history too, and it does nothing to stop the pollution happening in the first place.
whyWrong.D: CLAUDE.md is loaded into every session, so this adds cost everywhere, and the analysis would still run in the main context and flood it.

questions.mindset: Isolate verbose or exploratory work structurally; don't ask the model to be quieter.

questions.stem: A platform team has two pieces of guidance to give Claude Code. (1) A one-line rule that every TypeScript file in the monorepo must use named exports, never default exports. (2) A 40-step procedure for cutting a quarterly release, which includes tagging, changelog generation and publishing packages, and which should only ever run when a release manager deliberately starts it. Which TWO configuration choices are MOST appropriate? Choose TWO.

options.text: Put both items in the project CLAUDE.md so Claude always has the complete picture regardless of what the developer is working on.
Put the named-exports rule in the project CLAUDE.md, because it is a universal standard that should apply to every session.
Write the release procedure into CLAUDE.md under an IMPORTANT heading so Claude reliably follows every step when a release is mentioned.
Package the named-exports rule as a skill so it is loaded only when Claude decides it is relevant, which saves context in every session.
Package the release procedure as a project skill with `disable-model-invocation: true`, so it is loaded and run only when someone invokes it.

questions.explanation: CLAUDE.md is for short, universal standards that should be in context every session, which fits the named-exports rule. Skills are for on-demand, task-specific workflows: only their name and description sit in context until invoked. Because the release has side effects and must start deliberately, `disable-model-invocation: true` makes it user-invocable only.

whyWrong.A: Loading a 40-step procedure into every session wastes context and dilutes the instructions that matter. Docs warn that a bloated CLAUDE.md causes rules to get lost.
whyWrong.C: Emphasis does not make a long, rarely used procedure belong in always-loaded memory, and it does nothing to stop the procedure from being triggered unintentionally.
whyWrong.D: A rule that applies to every TypeScript file should not depend on Claude deciding a skill is relevant. A one-line universal rule costs almost nothing in CLAUDE.md.

questions.mindset: Always-true standards go in CLAUDE.md; occasional procedures go in on-demand skills.

questions.scenario: Scenario: Code Generation with Claude Code. Your team uses Claude Code for code generation, refactoring, debugging and documentation, and is wiring it into the development workflow with custom slash commands, skills and CLAUDE.md configuration.
questions.stem: The repository ships a project skill at `.claude/skills/pr-summary/SKILL.md` that the whole team uses. One senior engineer wants a much terser version for personal use. They also want to keep running the team's version when posting official summaries, and must not change anything their teammates see. What should they do?

options.text: Edit `.claude/skills/pr-summary/SKILL.md` in a local branch to make it terser, and simply avoid pushing that change to the remote repository.
Add instructions to their `CLAUDE.local.md` telling Claude to make PR summaries terse whenever the `/pr-summary` skill is invoked.
Create `~/.claude/skills/pr-summary/SKILL.md` with the terser instructions, so their personal copy is used in place of the team version.
Create a personal skill under a different name, such as `~/.claude/skills/pr-summary-terse/SKILL.md`, and leave the team skill untouched.

questions.explanation: A personal skill in `~/.claude/skills/` affects only that user. Giving it a **different name** means both `/pr-summary` (team) and `/pr-summary-terse` (personal) stay available and nothing changes for teammates. This is the personal-variant pattern in the exam guide.

whyWrong.A: An uncommitted edit to a tracked project file is fragile: it is easy to commit by accident, it conflicts with upstream changes, and the engineer loses the unmodified team version in their own checkout.
whyWrong.B: CLAUDE.local.md adds always-loaded advisory context. It can conflict with the skill's own instructions, and it changes the team skill's behaviour for this user instead of giving them a separate variant.
whyWrong.C: When a personal and a project skill share a name, the personal one takes priority. The engineer could no longer run the team's `/pr-summary`, which breaks their requirement to keep using it.

questions.mindset: Customize for yourself with a separately named personal variant; never shadow or fork shared config.

questions.scenario: Scenario: Code Generation with Claude Code. Your team uses Claude Code for code generation, refactoring, debugging and documentation, and is wiring it into the development workflow with custom slash commands, skills and CLAUDE.md configuration.
questions.stem: A `/migrate-component` skill converts a React class component to a function component. It works well when invoked as `/migrate-component src/Button.tsx`. Engineers often type just `/migrate-component`, and Claude then picks whatever file looks relevant from the conversation, sometimes the wrong one. The team wants engineers to be reminded at invocation time which parameter the skill expects. What is the MOST direct fix?

options.text: Add two or three few-shot examples to SKILL.md that show the skill being run correctly on different component files.
Add `argument-hint: [component-file]` to the frontmatter and reference the value in the body with `$ARGUMENTS`.
Rename the skill to `/migrate-component-file` so the name itself makes it obvious that a file path is required.
Add a note to the project CLAUDE.md telling developers to always pass a file path when they call the migration skill.

questions.explanation: `argument-hint` is the frontmatter field that shows the expected arguments during autocomplete, so the developer sees `[component-file]` while typing the command. `$ARGUMENTS` substitutes what they pass into the skill body. This targets the gap at the point where the mistake is made.

whyWrong.A: Examples help Claude understand the transformation, but they do not prompt the developer for the missing parameter at invocation time.
whyWrong.C: A longer name is an indirect hint at best. Autocomplete still shows no parameter, and existing muscle memory breaks.
whyWrong.D: CLAUDE.md is context for Claude, not a prompt shown to developers while they type. It also loads into every session for a single skill's concern.

questions.mindset: Use the built-in frontmatter control made for the job before inventing workarounds.

questions.stem: A project skill `deploy-staging` builds the app and pushes it to the shared staging environment. Several times this week, an engineer mentioned staging in passing ("the staging data looks stale") and Claude decided the skill was relevant and started a deployment. The team wants the skill to keep working when someone deliberately types `/deploy-staging`, and wants it to be impossible for Claude to start this skill on its own. What should they change?

options.text: Reword the skill's description to say "Use only when the user explicitly asks to deploy to staging" so Claude stops selecting it on its own.
Add `context: fork` so the deployment runs in an isolated subagent and cannot be influenced by casual mentions in the main chat.
Set `disable-model-invocation: true` in the skill's frontmatter so that only a user can invoke it with `/deploy-staging`.
Move the skill to each engineer's `~/.claude/skills/` directory so it is no longer part of the shared project configuration.

questions.explanation: `disable-model-invocation: true` removes the skill from what Claude can trigger on its own, so it runs only when a user types `/deploy-staging`. Docs recommend this for workflows with side effects. It is a configuration guarantee, not a hint.

whyWrong.A: A carefully worded description lowers the odds but leaves the decision with the model. The requirement says unrequested deployment must be impossible, which calls for a deterministic control.
whyWrong.B: `context: fork` changes where the skill runs, not who can trigger it. Claude could still invoke it automatically.
whyWrong.D: Moving it to personal directories breaks sharing and version control, and Claude can still auto-invoke a personal skill.

questions.mindset: When a behaviour must never happen, use a configuration guarantee rather than better wording.

questions.stem: A `/commit-work` skill stages and commits changes. Engineers complain that every run stops for approval prompts on `git add` and `git commit`. Security also requires that Claude must never run `git push`, during this skill or at any other time. Which TWO changes together meet both requirements? Choose TWO.

options.text: Add `allowed-tools: Bash(git add *) Bash(git commit *)` to the skill frontmatter so those commands run without prompting in the turn that invokes the skill.
Rely on the `allowed-tools` list alone, because listing only `git add` and `git commit` blocks every other command, including `git push`.
Add a bold line to SKILL.md saying "Never run git push under any circumstances" so Claude stays within the allowed workflow.
Add a deny rule such as `Bash(git push *)` to the permissions in the project's `.claude/settings.json`, so push is blocked in every session.
Add `context: fork` so the skill runs in an isolated subagent whose separate context has no access to push commands.

questions.explanation: `allowed-tools` **pre-approves** the listed tools for the turn that invokes the skill (the grant clears on your next message), which removes the prompts. The docs state explicitly that it does not restrict which tools are available. The guarantee that push never runs therefore has to come from a permission **deny** rule in settings, which applies in every session, not only while the skill runs. `Bash(git push *)` (equivalently `Bash(git push:*)`) is the documented pattern; the docs note it matches commands that begin with `git push`, so for an airtight control you would pair it with sandboxing, but among the options only a deny rule is a deterministic control at all.

whyWrong.B: Per the skills docs, `allowed-tools` does not restrict anything: every tool remains callable, and normal permission settings govern the rest. Relying on it as a sandbox leaves push reachable.
whyWrong.C: A prompt instruction is advisory. A hard security requirement needs a deterministic control such as a deny rule.
whyWrong.E: A forked subagent changes the context, not the permissions. It still works under the session's permission rules and is not barred from Bash.

questions.mindset: Pre-approval removes friction; only deny rules (or hooks) give guarantees.

questions.scenario: Scenario: Developer Productivity with Claude. You are building developer productivity tooling on Claude Code and the Agent SDK that helps engineers explore unfamiliar codebases, understand legacy systems, generate boilerplate and automate repetitive tasks using the built-in tools and MCP servers.
questions.stem: Your internal `/api-client-gen` skill generates typed API clients. Over six months its SKILL.md has grown to about 1,400 lines, including the full error-code catalogue, every endpoint's quirks and long worked examples. Whenever the skill is invoked, a large chunk of context is used up at once, even for simple endpoints that need none of that reference material. What is the BEST way to restructure it?

options.text: Keep the core workflow in a short SKILL.md and move the reference material into supporting files in the skill directory that SKILL.md links to, so they load only when needed.
Split the skill into six smaller skills with overlapping descriptions so Claude can choose whichever one seems to match the endpoint being generated at the time.
Move the error-code catalogue and endpoint quirks into the project CLAUDE.md so the reference material is already in context before the skill is ever invoked.
Add `context: fork` so the oversized SKILL.md loads inside a subagent and the main conversation is protected from its size whenever the skill runs.

questions.explanation: Skills use progressive disclosure. The name and description are always listed, the SKILL.md body loads on invocation, and supporting files load only when Claude needs them. Docs advise keeping SKILL.md under 500 lines and moving detailed reference material into separate files referenced from SKILL.md.

whyWrong.B: Overlapping descriptions make selection ambiguous, and each extra skill adds a listing entry to every session. It's a more complex design that doesn't fix the root cause.
whyWrong.C: CLAUDE.md loads in every session, so this makes context use worse everywhere, not only when generating clients.
whyWrong.D: Forking moves the cost into a subagent but still loads all 1,400 lines every time, and the subagent's work quality suffers from the same bloat. It hides the symptom instead of fixing the structure.

questions.mindset: Load detail just in time: a lean entry file plus on-demand supporting files.

questions.scenario: Scenario: Structured Data Extraction. A team is using Claude Code to build and refine the transformation code behind a pipeline that turns unstructured vendor documents into validated JSON for downstream systems.
questions.stem: An engineer asks Claude Code to write a normalizer for the `invoice_date` field. The prompt says: "Convert dates to a standard ISO format, handling the usual regional variations sensibly." Across three attempts Claude reads `03/04/2025` as 3 April in one version and 4 March in another, and handles two-digit years inconsistently. What should the engineer do FIRST to get consistent behaviour?

options.text: Expand the prose with several paragraphs describing what "sensibly" means for each regional date convention Claude is likely to encounter.
Switch to a larger model for this task, since resolving date-parsing ambiguity needs stronger reasoning than the current model is showing.
Ask Claude to double-check its own output after each attempt and confirm that every date in the sample has been parsed correctly.
Give two or three concrete input/output pairs, such as `03/04/2025` → `2025-04-03` and `7-Jan-99` → `1999-01-07`, that pin down the mapping.

questions.explanation: When a natural-language description is interpreted inconsistently, 2–3 concrete input/output examples are the most effective way to show the exact transformation. Examples settle the ambiguity (day-first vs month-first, how to read two-digit years) that prose leaves open.

whyWrong.A: More prose gives Claude more to interpret and does not remove the core ambiguity. Examples state the answer directly.
whyWrong.B: The problem is an underspecified requirement, not model capability. A larger model would still have to guess which convention you want.
whyWrong.C: Self-checking against an ambiguous spec only confirms whichever reading Claude already chose. Self-review doesn't add the missing information.

questions.mindset: When prose is ambiguous, show examples instead of adding more prose.

questions.scenario: Scenario: Code Generation with Claude Code. Your team uses Claude Code for code generation, refactoring, debugging and documentation, and is wiring it into the development workflow with custom slash commands, skills and CLAUDE.md configuration.
questions.stem: An engineer needs Claude Code to implement a token-bucket rate limiter for an API gateway. The requirements include burst handling, correct behaviour when the clock goes backwards, and a ceiling of 1 ms per check under load. Earlier attempts "looked right" in review but failed in staging on edge cases. Which workflow will MOST reliably drive the implementation to a correct result?

options.text: Have Claude implement the limiter first, then ask it to review its own code carefully for edge cases and rate its confidence in each path before merging.
Have Claude write tests first covering normal behaviour, the edge cases and the latency ceiling, then implement and iterate by sharing the test failures.
Write a detailed natural-language specification that covers every requirement and ask Claude to implement it in one careful pass, with no tests.
Use plan mode to design the limiter, approve the plan, then rely on code review in the pull request to catch any edge cases that were missed.

questions.explanation: Test-driven iteration gives Claude a check it can run. Tests for expected behaviour, edge cases and performance are written first, then each iteration feeds back concrete failures until everything passes. The docs stress that without a runnable check, "looks done" is the only signal, which is exactly how the earlier attempts failed.

whyWrong.A: Self-review and self-rated confidence aren't an objective signal. The model grades its own work against its own assumptions, which already missed these edge cases once.
whyWrong.C: A detailed spec helps, but with no tests there is still nothing that produces a pass or fail. The edge-case failures would surface in staging again.
whyWrong.D: Planning is useful for choosing an approach, but a plan does not verify behaviour, and human PR review is exactly what already failed to catch these edge cases.

questions.mindset: Give the model an objective check to iterate against, and write it before the code.

questions.scenario: Scenario: Developer Productivity with Claude. You are building developer productivity tooling on Claude Code and the Agent SDK that helps engineers explore unfamiliar codebases, understand legacy systems, generate boilerplate and automate repetitive tasks using the built-in tools and MCP servers.
questions.stem: An engineer is asked to add a caching layer in front of a legacy pricing service they have never worked on. Prices change on a schedule that nobody has documented, and some downstream consumers can't tolerate stale data. The engineer is unsure what they don't know. Which approach BEST surfaces the important design considerations before any code is written?

options.text: Ask Claude to interview them first about invalidation, staleness tolerance, failure modes and consumers, then capture the answers as a spec before implementing.
Ask Claude to implement a standard time-based cache right away, then fix whatever problems the downstream consumers report once it reaches staging.
Ask Claude to implement the cache and then list every assumption it made about invalidation and staleness, so the engineer can review those afterwards.
Spawn several subagents to research caching best practices and invalidation strategies on the web, then merge their findings into the implementation prompt.

questions.explanation: The interview pattern has Claude ask questions before implementing, which surfaces considerations the developer hasn't anticipated in an unfamiliar domain, such as cache invalidation strategy and failure modes. Docs recommend having Claude interview you (for example with `AskUserQuestion`) and writing the result into a spec.

whyWrong.B: Building first and discovering requirements from production complaints is the rework this pattern exists to avoid, and stale prices may reach consumers who can't tolerate them.
whyWrong.C: Listing assumptions after implementation catches problems too late. The design may already rest on a wrong invalidation strategy.
whyWrong.D: Generic web research doesn't know this service's undocumented price schedule or its consumers' tolerances. The missing knowledge sits with the engineer and their stakeholders.

questions.mindset: In unfamiliar territory, have the model ask questions before it builds anything.

questions.stem: While refining a data migration with Claude Code, an engineer finds three problems: (1) the migration writes `created_at` in server-local time; (2) the reporting query that reads that same column assumes UTC and buckets rows by day; (3) a log message in an unrelated retry helper has a typo. Fixing (1) changes what (2) must do. How should the engineer structure the feedback? Choose TWO.

options.text: Report all three issues as one-line comments in a single message so Claude can fix everything in one pass.
Fix issue (2) first on its own, observe the report output, and only then raise issue (1) in a later message.
Describe issues (1) and (2) together in one detailed message that explains how they interact and what the end-to-end result should be.
Ask Claude to fix the issues one at a time in the order they were found, verifying each fix before raising the next one.
Handle the typo in (3) as its own separate fix, in a different message from the timezone work, either before or after it.

questions.explanation: Issues whose fixes interact should go in a **single detailed message**, so Claude can design one consistent change (for example, store UTC and adjust the query's bucketing together) instead of fixing one half against a moving target. Independent issues are best handled **sequentially**, so each change stays small, easy to verify and easy to rewind. The typo has nothing to do with the timezone work, so it is its own step. This is the exam guide's stated rule for task 3.5 and matches the docs' advice to keep feedback loops tight and verifiable.

whyWrong.A: Bundling an unrelated typo with terse notes hides the key interaction between (1) and (2), and makes the result harder to verify.
whyWrong.B: Fixing the query alone, against data that is about to change, guarantees rework. The two fixes have to be designed together.
whyWrong.D: Strict one-at-a-time ordering splits (1) and (2), so the first fix is made without knowing the constraint the second one imposes.

questions.mindset: Batch interacting problems into one message; iterate on independent ones separately.

questions.stem: A customer-table migration script that Claude Code wrote crashes partway through production-like test data. The cause is records where `middle_name` is null, and some where it is an empty string. The engineer's first follow-up, "Please make the script handle edge cases robustly", produced a version that silently skips any row with a missing field. What is the MOST effective next message?

options.text: Repeat the request more firmly, stating that the script must handle every possible edge case correctly without skipping any rows at all.
Ask Claude to wrap the per-row logic in a try/except that logs and continues, so the migration always completes end to end.
Give test cases with input and expected output, e.g. `middle_name: null` → `NULL`, `""` → `NULL`, and state that no rows may be dropped.
Ask Claude to review the whole script line by line and list every edge case it can think of in the data before changing anything.

questions.explanation: Specific test cases with example input and expected output state exactly how each edge case must be handled, which removes the room for interpretation that produced the row-skipping "fix". They also give Claude a checkable target for the next iteration.

whyWrong.A: Stating the vague request more firmly doesn't define the correct behaviour for null versus empty values.
whyWrong.B: Catch-and-continue hides the defect and still loses data. It treats the symptom, not the root cause.
whyWrong.D: A self-generated edge-case list may be useful, but it doesn't tell Claude what the right output is for the case that actually broke.

questions.mindset: Pin down edge cases with concrete input → expected output, not adjectives.

questions.stem: An engineer has spent 40 minutes in one Claude Code session trying to get a CSV exporter to quote fields correctly. They have corrected Claude four times. Each attempt fixes one case and breaks another, and the conversation is now full of abandoned approaches. What should they do next to make the most progress?

options.text: Keep correcting in the same session, writing future corrections in capital letters so the important constraint stands out.
Run `/compact` so the history is summarized, then continue issuing corrections in the same session.
Switch to plan mode inside the same session and ask Claude to reconsider its approach before making further edits.
Run `/clear` and start fresh with a more specific prompt that includes what was learned, such as example rows with expected quoted output.

questions.explanation: Docs call out "correcting over and over" as a failure pattern: the context fills with failed approaches. Their rule is that once you have corrected Claude more than twice on the same issue, run `/clear` and start fresh with a more specific prompt that incorporates what you learned, because a clean session with a better prompt almost always outperforms a long session with accumulated corrections. Concrete example rows with expected quoted output make the new prompt much sharper.

whyWrong.A: Emphasis doesn't remove the polluted context that is causing the back-and-forth.
whyWrong.B: Compaction keeps a summary of the failed approaches, so the confusion carries over, and no new, specific information is added.
whyWrong.C: Planning inside the same cluttered session still reasons over the abandoned attempts. The fix is to restart clean with a better prompt.

questions.mindset: A clean session with a better prompt beats a long session of accumulated corrections.

questions.scenario: Scenario: Claude Code for Continuous Integration. Claude Code runs in your CI/CD pipeline to review pull requests, generate test cases and post feedback. The team wants actionable output with few false positives.
questions.stem: In your CI pipeline, Claude Code generates unit tests for a new `parseTariff()` function, runs them and posts results on the pull request. On the first iteration, 3 of 22 generated tests fail, and two of the failures involve a tariff code with a trailing whitespace character. The workflow can send one follow-up message back to Claude. Which TWO kinds of content in that message will MOST effectively drive the next iteration? Choose TWO.

options.text: The exact names of the failing tests, with their assertion output (expected versus actual values) copied from the test runner.
A general instruction to "try harder and be more careful this time", since the first attempt was mostly correct.
A concrete example input with its expected output for the whitespace case, such as `"TX-104 "` → `{ code: "TX-104" }`.
A request to discard the current implementation and rewrite `parseTariff()` from scratch using a completely different algorithm.
A request for Claude to add verbose logging everywhere and give a confidence score for each test before rerunning.

questions.explanation: Iterative refinement works best when the feedback is concrete and checkable. Sharing the specific test failures (names plus expected versus actual) tells Claude exactly what is wrong, and a specific input → expected output example for the edge case removes ambiguity about the intended behaviour.

whyWrong.B: An exhortation carries no information about what failed or why.
whyWrong.D: Rewriting from scratch throws away 19 passing tests' worth of correct behaviour to fix a narrow, well-located defect.
whyWrong.E: Logging and self-rated confidence add noise and an unreliable signal. They don't say what the correct behaviour should be.

questions.mindset: Feed back exact failures and exact expectations, not effort or confidence.

questions.scenario: Scenario: Code Generation with Claude Code. Your team uses Claude Code for code generation, refactoring, debugging and documentation, and is wiring it into the development workflow with custom slash commands, skills and CLAUDE.md configuration.
questions.stem: An engineer used the interview pattern in a long Claude Code session: Claude asked about 30 questions on a new webhook-retry feature, and together they produced a detailed `SPEC.md` covering retries, idempotency keys, ordering and what is out of scope. The session's context is now mostly that Q&A. The engineer wants the implementation to follow the spec closely and be verifiable. What is the BEST next step?

options.text: Continue in the same session immediately, because all the reasoning behind each decision is still in context and will help with implementation.
Start a fresh session, point Claude at `SPEC.md` and have it implement the feature along with tests that verify the spec end to end.
Run `/compact` in the current session and then ask Claude to implement the feature from its compacted memory of the discussion.
Paste the full interview transcript into a new session alongside `SPEC.md` so no nuance from the discussion is lost.

questions.explanation: Docs recommend that once the interview has produced a complete spec, you start a fresh session to execute it. The new session has clean context focused on implementation, and the written, self-contained spec (ideally ending in an end-to-end verification step) is the source of truth.

whyWrong.A: The Q&A is mostly noise for implementation and takes up context. Performance degrades as context fills, and the decisions are already captured in `SPEC.md`.
whyWrong.C: A compacted summary is lossy, while the precise written spec is authoritative. Implementing from memory of a summary invites drift.
whyWrong.D: Re-adding the whole transcript brings back the clutter the fresh session was meant to remove. The spec exists to distil it.

questions.mindset: Separate discovery from execution: capture the spec, then implement in a clean context.
